Multiobjective Optimization Approaches for Room Allocation in
University Course Timetabling✩
Bruno Antunes-Batistaa, Soumen Attab,∗, Vítor Basto-Fernandesa,c,1, Iryna Yevseyevad,
Michael Emmerichb
aInstituto Universitário de Lisboa (ISCTE-IUL), ISTAR, 1649-026 Lisboa, Portugal
bFaculty of Information Technology, University of Jyväskylä, P.O. Box 35 (Agora), Jyväskylä, 40014, Finland

Abstract
This study addresses the complex and time-consuming task of room allocation in university timetabling, which, despite the avail-
ability of software tools, is still predominantly performed manually due to the inefficiency of existing solutions. The adoption of
such software remains limited, primarily due to complex parameter configurations and the lack of institutional customization. This
paper focuses on the room allocation subproblem of the University Course Timetabling Problem (UCTP) and defines six criteria:
four objectives to minimize student relocation between buildings, mismatches between requested and assigned room types, waste
of room capacity and room changes between consecutive classes, and two hard constraints to ensure that room capacity require-
ments are respected and to prevent scheduling overlaps. Customized variants of NSGA-II, NSGA-III, and MOEA/D, tailored to
the room allocation context, were developed using the jMetal framework with integrated local search. Experiments were conducted
using real-world data from a university over a full academic semester, involving approximately 10,000 students, more than 26,000
scheduled class sessions, and over 120 classrooms distributed across multiple buildings with over 20 distinct room types. The cus-
tomized multiobjective evolutionary algorithms were compared against an integer linear programming (ILP) formulation modeled
in Pyomo and solved using Gurobi.

1. Introduction
Efficient academic timetable management plays a critical role in the operational success of higher education insti-
tutions. The University Course Timetabling Problem (UCTP) is recognized as a complex combinatorial optimization
problem of NP-hard nature [1, 4]. The scale of the problem, combined with the limitations of existing software so-
lutions in terms of scalability, customization, and performance, highlights the need for a more robust and institution-
specific approach.
Classical methods based on Integer Linear Programming (ILP) and mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) of-
fer precise formulations but suffer from computational intractability for large-scale instances. In contrast, population-
based metaheuristics such as Genetic Algorithm (GA) and Ant Colony Optimization (ACO) have demonstrated su-
perior performance on large and complex timetabling problems [4, 13]. Recent literature, including works by Chen
et al. [4] and Bashab et al. [2], emphasizes the effectiveness of hybrid approaches that combine global metaheuristic
search with local intensification strategies. These methods, particularly evolutionary algorithms [14] like NSGA-II [7],
NSGA-III [6, 12], and MOEA/D [17], have shown promising results in handling multiple conflicting criteria simulta-
neously.
Motivated by these findings, this work proposes and compares two approaches to solving room allocation in UCTP:
an ILP-based model, which aims to find optimal solutions under strict constraints, and a multiobjective evolutionary
algorithm framework, implemented in jMetal [8, 9], which incorporates local search and constructive heuristics for
initial solution generation to improve scalability and solution quality. The goal is to assess the effectiveness of both
methods in meeting institutional requirements and addressing the realistic scale of the timetabling problem in a uni-
versity.
This study is motivated by the need to address the UCTP through a comprehensive analysis of existing solution
methods and their applicability to real-world scenarios. To guide the investigation, several research questions were
formulated: (i) What are the most widely used approaches to solving the UCTP? (ii) What are their main advantages,
disadvantages, and limitations? (iii) What innovations and opportunities for improvement have been proposed in the
literature? (iv) What recent trends have emerged in the UCTP research? and (v) How do metaheuristic algorithms
compare to exact methods such as ILP? These questions serve as a foundation for understanding the current state-of-
the-art and identifying gaps that can be addressed through novel algorithmic strategies.
To answer these questions, the objectives of this work include identifying and analyzing the most widely used
techniques for solving UCTP and benchmarking selected algorithms using real-world data from a university. Partic-
ular emphasis is placed on comparing the performance of multiobjective evolutionary algorithms, such as NSGA-II,
NSGA-III, and MOEA/D, with ILP-based approaches, with the goal of evaluating their effectiveness in terms of
scalability, solution quality, and adaptability to institutional constraints.
This paper makes two contributions: (i) Scale-up: we study a large-scale real-world room allocation in UCTP at
a university for a semester, with more than 10,000 students, more than 26,000 classes and over 120 rooms in more
than 20 types, highlighting scalability and practicality beyond previously published studies (e.g., Torres-Ovalle et al.
[16]); (ii) Multiobjective decision support: we define six objectives to solve them using NSGA-II, NSGA-III, and
MOEA/D, paired with exact solvers and employ hypervolume-driven early stopping. This allows stakeholders to
evaluate different high-performing room allocations instead of a single aggregated solution.
The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 presents the description and mathematical formulation
of the problem. Section 3 outlines the proposed solution methodologies. Section 4 details the experimental setup and
discusses the results and key findings. Finally, Section 5 concludes the paper and outlines directions for future research.
2. Problem Description
The problem addressed in this work focuses on the UCTP room allocation subproblem. Specifically, it assumes that
the weekly timetable of classes is already defined and aims to assign classrooms to scheduled classes in a way that
minimizes the violation of four soft constraints while ensuring the satisfaction of two hard constraints. This variant
of the UCTP is practically relevant and computationally challenging, as it deals with optimizing room assignments
within fixed temporal slots.

Each room is characterized by a set of descriptive attributes, including
• Name: A unique room identifier;
• Capacity: The total number of available seats;
• Features: A set of characteristics such as regular classroom, computer lab, and others;
• Building: The building in which the room is located.
Formally, let R = {r1, r2, . . . , r|R|} denote the set of rooms, where each room r j ∈R is defined by the attributes listed
above. Each scheduled class is also described by the following attributes:
• Course: The academic program(s) to which the class belongs;
• Shift: The specific shift (e.g., morning, afternoon, evening) of the class;
• Class Name: A unique class identifier;
• Enrolled Students: The number of students registered for the class;
• Day and Time: The scheduled day, start time, and end time of the class;
• Requested Room Features: The required room features for the class.
Let C = {c1, c2, . . . , c|C|} represent the set of scheduled classes, where each class ci ∈C must be assigned to a
suitable room rj ∈R. The goal is to perform this assignment while respecting all hard constraints and minimizing the
penalties associated with soft constraint violations.
To formally represent the room allocation optimization problem, we define a set of penalized objective functions
corresponding to both soft and hard constraints. The soft constraints capture desirable properties of a good allocation
and are modeled as objectives (f1 to f4) to be minimized. Although hard constraints must be strictly satisfied in feasible
solutions, they are also expressed as penalized objective functions ( f5 and f6) to enable uniform treatment within a
multiobjective optimization framework. Next, we present the formulation of each objective function.

3. Proposed Solution Methodology
The proposed methodology for solving the room allocation of the UCTP is based on insights drawn from the
literature and findings of the systematic literature review. The approach combines multiobjective optimization, hy-

667
brid heuristics, and exact methods. Specifically, three evolutionary multiobjective algorithms, NSGA-II [7], NSGA-
III [6, 12], and MOEA/D [17], are applied due to their effectiveness in handling problems with multiple conflicting
criteria. To further enhance solution quality, hybrid versions of these algorithms are developed by integrating local
search techniques that intensify the search around promising individual solutions. Additionally, Integer Linear Pro-
gramming (ILP) [15] is used, serving as a benchmark for evaluating the quality of metaheuristic solutions. Finally, the
evolutionary process is initialized using both randomly generated solutions and heuristically constructed initial popu-
lations, with and without local refinement, to assess the impact of initial solution quality on the overall optimization
performance. We aim to evaluate the impact of heuristic solution construction and local search intensification on the
performance of evolutionary algorithms, and to demonstrate the robustness of hybrid methods in effectively solving
complex and large-scale scheduling problems, such as the real instance obtained from a university.
The implementation of the proposed solution methodologies involved the use of NSGA-II [7], NSGA-III [6, 12],
and MOEA/D [17] algorithms integrated into the jMetal [8, 9] framework, along with an ILP approach formulated
using the Pyomo [3, 11] modeling language and solved using the Gurobi [10] solver. Gurobi [10], available for free for
academic use, provided the required functionality. Customized variants of the evolutionary algorithms were developed
with integrated local search procedures to enhance solution quality. The jMetal framework was employed to manage
problem definitions, solution representations, genetic operators, and experimental evaluations. The implementation
was carried out in Java and Python, reflecting the tool chain: Java for jMetal and Python for Pyomo and Gurobi solver
integration.
The local search procedure was integrated into the evolutionary multiobjective algorithms using the
BasicLocalSearch class from the jMetal [8, 9] framework. This was configured with an Integer Polynomial Mu-
tation operator, a standard dominance comparator (DefaultDominanceComparator [8, 9]), and a reference to the
problem model. The mutation operator was parameterized with a mutation probability of 1
n, where n denotes the num-
ber of genes in a chromosome, and a distribution index of 20. In each iteration, the local search generated a single
neighbor solution. If the new solution dominated the current one according to the dominance comparator, it was ac-
cepted as the replacement. This mechanism enhanced the evolutionary process by introducing targeted improvements
in solution quality.
To enhance the quality of initial solutions and provide effective starting points for the evolutionary process, a
constructive heuristic was implemented. This method assigns each class to a room by prioritizing the satisfaction of
hard constraints. For each class ci ∈C, the heuristic iteratively selects the first room r j ∈R satisfying the follow-
ing conditions: capacity(rj) ≥students(ci)
and
¬overlap(ci, rj, Di), where capacity(rj) is the capacity of
room r j, students(ci) is the number of enrolled students in class ci, Di is the day on which the class occurs, and
overlap(ci, rj, Di) verifies whether another class already occupies room rj at the same time on day Di. If no feasible
room is found, a room is assigned randomly as r j ←rand(R).
Instead of relying on a fixed number of iterations as the stopping criterion, the proposed method incorporates
a dynamic mechanism based on the hypervolume [18] quality indicator. At each generation, the hypervolume of
the current Pareto front is computed and compared against the best value observed so far. If there is no significant
improvement over a predefined number of consecutive generations, the algorithm terminates early, thereby avoiding
unnecessary computations. Initially, the hypervolume of the first generation is recorded as the best value. During each
subsequent generation, the hypervolume of the current front is recalculated and compared with the stored best value. If
the improvement exceeds a small threshold value, set to 10−6, the best value is updated, and the counter for stagnation
is reset. Otherwise, the counter is incremented. The algorithm halts when either the maximum number of generations
is reached or the number of consecutive generations without improvement reaches a predefined limit of 100.
An ILP model is also developed in this work. The ILP model assigns classes to rooms while enforcing two hard
constraints: (i) no class is assigned to a room with insufficient capacity, and (ii) overlapping classes from being
scheduled in the same room at the same time is prevented. To guarantee feasibility in cases where no room satisfies
the requirements, a heavily penalized dummy room is introduced. For example, a course has 59 students enrolled
and requires a computer lab, but all available computer labs have a maximum capacity of only 50 seats. Without the
dummy room, such cases would make the model infeasible. Moreover, the ILP model treats the two hard constraints
(room capacity and room overlap) as strongly penalized objective functions (see Eq. (5) and Eq. (6)), allowing the
model to generate feasible solutions even when physical limitations exist. Then, the model incorporates a weighted-
sum objective function that minimizes penalties (f1 to f4) associated with soft constraints, and penalties ( f5 and f6)

4. Experimental Results and Discussions
The experiments were conducted on a machine equipped with an AMD Ryzen 7 7840HS processor featuring
8 physical cores and 16 logical threads, and 40 GB of RAM, running Windows 11 (64-bit). The development en-
vironment included IntelliJ IDEA for Java and Visual Studio Code for Python. The evolutionary algorithms were
implemented using the jMetal 6.1 framework [8, 9], while the ILP model was developed in Python 3.12 using the
Pyomo [3, 11] modeling language and solved with the Gurobi [10] optimizer.
Experimental settings. The experimental study was conducted using two distinct approaches to solve the room and
timetable allocation problem: evolutionary multiobjective optimization and integer linear programming. The evolu-
tionary approach employed three algorithms, NSGA-II [7], NSGA-III [6, 12], and MOEA/D [17], across all config-
urations. Four experimental setups were tested to evaluate the impact of hybridization through local search and the
use of a constructive initial population. In Experiment 1, both local search and a random initial population were used.
Experiment 2 excluded both local search and a constructive initial population. Experiment 3 combined both local
search and a constructive initial population. Lastly, Experiment 4 used a constructive initial population without local
search. Each experiment was executed with 25 independent runs to ensure robustness and comparability of the results.
Test instances. To validate the effectiveness of the proposed algorithms, a real-world problem instance was used. The
real-world data provided by a university represents a full academic semester. This instance includes approximately
10,000 students, over 26,000 scheduled classes, and more than 120 rooms of over 20 distinct types, such as auditori-
ums, laboratories, and standard classrooms. It captures the complexity and institutional constraints of the actual room
allocation problem and serves as a realistic benchmark for evaluating the scalability and robustness of the proposed
methods.
Parameters of evolutionary algorithms. The configuration parameters used in the evolutionary algorithms are sum-
marized as follows. All three algorithms, NSGA-II, NSGA-III, and MOEA/D, were executed with a population size of
200. NSGA-II and MOEA/D used a stopping criterion based on a maximum of 80,000 evaluations, while NSGA-III
was limited to 400 generations. For mutation, all algorithms applied polynomial mutation with a distribution index of
20.0 and a mutation probability of one divided by the number of genes in the individual. NSGA-II and NSGA-III used
the Integer Polynomial Mutation operator, whereas MOEA/D used the standard Polynomial Mutation operator. The
crossover operator was Integer Simulated Binary Crossover (SBX) for NSGA-II [7] and NSGA-III, and Differential
Evolution Crossover for MOEA/D [17], with corresponding parameters: a crossover probability of 0.9 and distribution
index of 18.0 for the SBX [5], and Crossover Rate (CR) equal to 0.5 and Scaling Factor (F) equal to 1.0 for differen-
tial evolution. Selection in NSGA-II and NSGA-III was based on the Ranking and Crowding Distance Comparator.
NSGA-III employed four reference point divisions, whereas MOEA/D used Chebychev decomposition.
Performance analysis of evolutionary algorithms. Table 1 presents the mean and standard deviation of the normal-
ized hypervolume (NHV) [18] and generalized spread (GSPREAD) [7] for MOEA/D, NSGA-II, and NSGA-III across
the four experimental configurations.
Overall, MOEA/D consistently achieved the best performance in terms of solution quality and stability across all
experiments, with NHV values close to 1.000 and low standard deviations, indicating highly converged and well-
distributed Pareto fronts. Its GSPREAD remained stable with slight variation, showing robustness to changes in local
search and initial population strategies. We believe it achieves higher hypervolume because its decomposition uses
dedicated weight vectors to cover extreme Pareto front points, and its Differential Evolution crossover creates larger
moves than SBX with polynomial mutation.
NSGA-II showed significant sensitivity to the experimental configurations. Its performance improved steadily from
Experiment 1 (NHV = 0.550) to Experiment 4 (NHV = 0.946), with the highest NHV observed when no hybridization

compact and well-distributed fronts, while performance slightly declined in Experiment 3 with local search and con-
structive population. We believe the crowding distance assignment struggles with a higher number of objectives.
NSGA-III exhibited unstable behavior with relatively low NHV values across all experiments. Its best NHV
(0.675) was recorded in Experiment 4, though with a high standard deviation, suggesting inconsistency across runs.
GSPREAD values were generally moderate, with the highest value in Experiment 1 (0.636), implying better diversity
when local search was applied without heuristic initialization.
In terms of runtime, Experiment 1, which used local search without a constructive population, had the longest
execution time at 16 hours and 40 minutes. Experiment 3, which combined both strategies, took 15 hours and 48
minutes to complete. Experiments 2 and 4 were comparatively faster, requiring 14 hours and 10 minutes and 13 hours
and 30 minutes, respectively. These results indicate that although hybridization can improve performance for some
algorithms, its effectiveness and computational cost vary notably between algorithmic configurations.

Figure 1 presents parallel coordinates plots comparing the results of four experiments. Across all experiments,
MOEA/D consistently exhibits high variability, particularly in hard constraints (corresponding to the functions f5 and
f6), while NSGA-II and NSGA-III show more stable and cohesive behavior. In Experiment 1, MOEA/D achieves
extreme solutions but with global instability; NSGA-II and NSGA-III demonstrate consistency, and the ILP shows
excellent constraint satisfaction but lacks solution diversity. In Experiment 2, the introduction of a heuristic-based
initial population improves feasibility for all algorithms, with MOEA/D maintaining its high-performing extremes
despite instability. Experiment 3 confirms previous patterns and shows limited gains from local search, as the initial
population already yields high-quality solutions. Finally, Experiment 4 demonstrates MOEA/D’s strong exploratory
ability even without intensification, while the lack of a good initial population reduces solution diversity. Across all
cases, ILP solutions remain stable and competitive on hard constraints but are limited to a single non-diverse solution.
5. Conclusion and Future Work
This study addressed the room allocation subproblem in university course timetabling, focusing on overcoming
the limitations of manual scheduling and the constrained adaptability of existing software. A set of four objectives
and two hard constraints was formulated to reflect practical institutional requirements. To solve this multiobjective
combinatorial problem, customized NSGA-II, NSGA-III, and MOEA/D were developed using the jMetal framework
with integrated local search, specifically adapted to the room allocation context. These were compared against an
integer linear programming (ILP) model formulated in Pyomo and solved with Gurobi.
Experimental results on real-world data from a full academic semester of a university demonstrated that ILP con-
sistently yielded high-quality feasible solutions, particularly for hard constraints, while the evolutionary algorithms
effectively explored diverse trade-offs among conflicting objectives. MOEA/D showed notably strong convergence
and spread, especially when enhanced with heuristic initialization and local search.
In the future, we plan to incorporate real-world constraints, like lecturer availability and room adjacency. Addi-
tionally, combining ILP and metaheuristics via hybrid or decomposition frameworks could enhance scalability and
solution quality for large-scale timetabling problems. Furthermore, future work will have to prioritize constructing a
broader set of benchmark data for large-scale problem solving using a posteriori multiobjective optimization to assess
method reliability across various problem instances.
